sections.h2: Who records a deed in Bourbon County, Kentucky?
sections.html:
The Bourbon County Clerk records it, in the courthouse annex at 301 Main Street, Room 106, in Paris. Kentucky law sends a deed to the clerk of the county where the land sits, so a house on a Paris street and a horse farm near Millersburg both go through this one office.

The office lists weekday hours of 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with a later close of 6:00 p.m. on Thursday, and a phone line at (859) 987-2142, extension 236. The county directory puts the Property Valuation Administrator down the hall in Room 15 and the sheriff, who collects tax bills, in Room 104. That short hallway matters when you sell: the deed, the assessment record and the tax bill all live within a few doors of each other.

sections.h2: What does Bourbon County sit on, and why does that matter for a deed?
sections.html:
Bourbon County covers about 290 square miles of gently rolling farmland in the Lexington area, with Paris as the seat and Millersburg and North Middletown as the other incorporated towns. It is one of Kentucky's nine original counties, formed in 1785.

Records here have a rough history. The courthouse burned in 1872 and again in 1901, and county records were lost each time, which is part of why a clean chain of title is worth checking before you sign a contract. The clerk's land records are the place a buyer's title company reads that chain, and an old gap in a legal description can slow a closing.

  • Large tracts and farm parcels often carry older legal descriptions that title examiners want to read line by line.
  • Easements, leases and plats are recorded documents too, and each has its own line on the fee schedule.
  • A buyer's title company will search the clerk's index before closing, so recording problems surface early.

sections.h2: What are the recording fees at the Bourbon County Clerk?
sections.html:
The fee schedule posted on the clerk's site lists a deed at $50 and a deed of correction at $46. It is dated January 1, 2020 and carries a note that fees may vary slightly, so call the office for a current total before you send anything.

Selected Bourbon County Clerk recording fees (clerk fee schedule dated January 1, 2020)
DocumentFee
Deed$50.00
Deed of correction$46.00
Mortgage$80.00
Mortgage with MERS or assignment$126.00
Release of mortgage, full or partial$46.00
Affidavit of descent$50.00
Power of attorney$50.00
Will$47.00
Lis pendens notice$46.00

The schedule adds $3.00 for each page past the first five on most documents and $4.00 for each extra parcel or reference. A long farm deed with several tax parcels costs more than a one-page town lot deed.

sections.h2: How much is the transfer tax on a Bourbon County sale?
sections.html:
The state real estate transfer tax is $0.50 for each $500 of value or fraction of it, and the seller named in the deed owes it. The clerk collects it before accepting the deed for recording.

The Census Bureau lists $229,300 as the 2020 to 2024 median value of an owner-occupied home in Bourbon County. A sale at that price is 459 units of $500, so the tax would be $229.50. A $150,000 sale is 300 units and $150.00. The tax is computed on the value stated in the deed, which includes any lien amounts for a sale that is not a gift.

Kentucky lists a number of transfers that owe no tax. The ones sellers ask about most:

  • A foreclosure transfer, or a voluntary surrender in lieu of foreclosure.
  • A transfer between spouses, or between former spouses in a divorce.
  • A transfer between parent and child, or grandparent and grandchild, for only nominal consideration.
  • A deed that only confirms or corrects a deed already recorded.

sections.h2: What must a deed contain before the Bourbon County Clerk will file it?
sections.html:
The clerk cannot file a deed that leaves out the items Kentucky requires. Those are the full names and mailing addresses of the grantor and grantee, a statement of the full consideration, and an in-care-of address for the current year's tax bill.

A sale also needs a sworn, notarized certificate, signed by both sides or their agents, that the price in the deed is the full price paid. A gift needs a similar certificate stating that it is a gift, with an estimated fair cash value. The deed must name the source of the seller's title, either the book and page of a recorded deed or a plain account of how the seller inherited it. Most sellers hand this to the title company or a Kentucky attorney, who drafts the deed to match.

sections.h2: What if the Bourbon County house came through an estate?
sections.html:
The personal representative files an affidavit with the county clerk listing who receives each property and its value, before the estate is closed. The clerk's schedule lists an affidavit of descent at $50.

This step often decides whether an inherited Paris house can sell quickly. A buyer's title company wants the chain from the deceased owner to the heirs in the Bourbon County records before it will insure a purchase. If the estate has not filed, start there, and ask the clerk's office which documents your situation needs.

sections.h2: What liens and notices does the clerk record against a Bourbon County property?
sections.html:
The clerk's website describes a long list of recorded claims, and any of them can show up in a title search. They include mechanics liens, judgment liens, lis pendens notices, federal and state tax liens and child support liens.

  • A judgment lien needs the court, case number and amount, and the clerk's page says the creditor or attorney signs it.
  • A lis pendens warns that title is in litigation and must name the court and action number.
  • A mechanics lien needs a notarized statement of the amount due and a property description specific enough to identify the parcel.
  • Each lien has its own release document, which is also recorded for a fee.

A seller who knows of one should ask the lienholder for a written payoff and a release, so the closing agent can pay it from proceeds and record the release afterward.

sections.h2: What do the numbers say about selling a house in Bourbon County?
sections.html:
Bourbon County had an estimated 20,243 residents in 2025 and about 9,399 housing units. Census figures for 2020 to 2024 show 63.7% of homes owner-occupied, a median gross rent of $822 and a median household income of $61,354. The mean commute is 25.4 minutes, which fits a county where many residents work in nearby Lexington.

A seller dealing with a house that needs repairs, a tenant, or a stalled estate has plenty of company in a county this size. The recording steps are the same either way, so the deed, transfer tax and any releases are the part you control.

faqs.q: Where is the Bourbon County Clerk's office?
faqs.a: It is at 301 Main Street, Room 106, in Paris, Kentucky. The county directory lists weekday hours of 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., open until 6:00 p.m. on Thursday.

faqs.q: How much does the clerk charge to record a deed in Bourbon County?
faqs.a: The clerk's posted schedule lists $50 for a deed and $46 for a deed of correction, with $3 for each page past five. That schedule is dated January 1, 2020, so confirm the current amount with the office.

faqs.q: Who pays the Kentucky transfer tax on a Bourbon County sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays it. The tax is $0.50 for each $500 of value, and the clerk collects it before recording the deed.

faqs.q: Does a deed in lieu of foreclosure owe the transfer tax?
faqs.a: No. Kentucky exempts a transfer made in a foreclosure proceeding or by a voluntary surrender in lieu of foreclosure. The mortgage holder must file that deed within 45 days after it is signed.

faqs.q: Can I record a deed in Bourbon County if the property is in another county?
faqs.a: No. A deed must be recorded with the clerk of the county where the property, or most of it, is located. A property split across a county line is recorded where the greater part lies.
